title: Putin Will Be in New Delhi in September. For NRIs Watching India’s Tightrope Walk, the Stakes Have Never Been Higher.
excerpt: The Kremlin has confirmed the Russian president will attend the BRICS summit on September 12-13 — his second India visit in under a year — as Trump’s 50% tariffs and the revival of the Russia-India-China troika reshape the global order.
body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin will travel to New Delhi on September 12-13 for the 18th BRICS summit, his aide confirmed this week — making it his second visit to India in under a year and his most symbolically charged trip to the subcontinent since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The visit comes at a moment when the diplomatic ground beneath India’s feet is shifting faster than at any point since independence. The United States has hiked tariffs on Indian goods to 50 per cent, explicitly linking the punishment to India’s continued purchase of Russian oil. China and India are slowly thawing a border standoff that froze relations for five years. And Moscow is openly pushing to revive the Russia-India-China (RIC) troika — a format that has been dormant since the 2020 Galwan Valley clash.

## What India Gets — and What It Risks

For Prime Minister Narendra Modi, hosting Putin is a statement of strategic autonomy at a time when Washington is trying to force a binary choice. India has, over the past decade, moved dramatically closer to the United States through frameworks like the Quad and major defence deals. But New Delhi has refused to abandon its relationship with Moscow, which supplies roughly 60 per cent of India’s defence hardware and has become one of its largest crude oil suppliers since the war in Ukraine upended global energy markets.

National Security Advisor Ajit Doval visited Moscow ahead of the summit announcement. While the specific agenda remains unclear, the visit is expected to cover defence procurement, energy cooperation, and India’s role as BRICS chair for 2026. The summit theme — ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’ — is diplomatically anodyne, but the subtext is unmistakable: the BRICS bloc, now expanded to 11 members, is positioning itself as an alternative to Western-dominated institutions.

## The RIC Wild Card

The most consequential element of Putin’s visit may be what happens on the sidelines. Russia has spent months lobbying for the revival of the RIC format, which was initiated in the 1990s by former Russian Prime Minister Yevgeny Primakov as a counterbalance to Western dominance. There have been 20 ministerial-level meetings over the years, but the format collapsed after the deadly border clash at Galwan in June 2020.

Now, the calculus has changed. All three RIC nations face economic pressure from Washington: India through tariffs, China through trade restrictions, and Russia through comprehensive sanctions. Modi is scheduled to visit China on August 31 for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, where he is expected to meet President Xi Jinping. If both the China and Russia tracks move forward, the RIC could re-emerge as a meaningful diplomatic grouping for the first time in half a decade.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the roughly 5 million Indian Americans — many of whom work in industries directly affected by US-India trade tensions — the BRICS summit is not an abstract geopolitical exercise. A deterioration in US-India relations would have immediate consequences for H-1B visa holders, Indian IT companies operating in America, and bilateral investment flows.

At the same time, India’s growing economic weight within the BRICS framework has implications for NRIs in the Gulf, Africa and Southeast Asia, where BRICS member states are major trade partners. The RBI has proposed including central bank digital currency (CBDC) interoperability on the BRICS agenda, which could reshape cross-border payments for the diaspora.

## What to Watch

The September summit will feature Chinese President Xi Jinping alongside Putin in New Delhi — a photo opportunity that would have been unthinkable two years ago. For Modi, the diplomatic choreography will matter as much as the substance. India needs to demonstrate that it can maintain its US partnership while simultaneously chairing a bloc that Russia views as a vehicle for challenging American hegemony.

The 50 per cent tariff, if it holds, gives India less room to manoeuvre than it had even six months ago. Whether the BRICS summit accelerates a genuine shift in global power dynamics — or remains a carefully staged display of symbolic unity — will depend largely on what Modi, Putin and Xi say to each other when the cameras are not rolling.
